title: Properties of Sound

competencies.text: Discuss properties of sound waves in communications, navigation, medicine, and entertainment.
Identify innovations such as soundproofing, amplifiers, and sonar.

days.title: How Sound Travels
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will discuss properties of sound waves in communication, navigation, medicine and entertainment, and identify innovations such as soundproofing, amplifiers and sonar.

🔊 Sound Is a Mechanical Wave

Sound is a vibration passed from particle to particle. It needs a medium — solid, liquid or gas — so it cannot travel through empty space.

Sound is a longitudinal wave: particles vibrate back and forth in the same direction the wave travels, forming compressions (crowded particles) and rarefactions (spread-out particles).

🏃 Speed of Sound

MediumApproximate speed
Air (20 °C)343 m/s
Water1,480 m/s
Steel5,960 m/s

Sound is fastest in solids, where particles are closest and most tightly linked. That is why you can hear an approaching train earlier by putting your ear near the rail (do not try it — it is dangerous).

Light is almost a million times faster than sound in air, so you see lightning before you hear thunder. Counting the seconds between them and multiplying by 343 m tells you roughly how far away the strike was.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: Astronauts on a spacewalk talk by radio, not by shouting. Why?

choices.label: Sound needs particles to travel through
Space suits block every kind of sound
Sound travels too fast in empty space
Radio waves are louder than voices

scenario.explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave; without air or another medium there are no particles to pass the vibration along. Radio waves are electromagnetic and cross empty space.

scenario.text: In which material does sound travel FASTEST?
scenario.explanation: Sound is fastest in solids (about 5,960 m/s in steel), slower in liquids and slowest in gases. It cannot travel in a vacuum.

scenario.text: You see lightning and hear thunder 3 seconds later. About how far away was the strike?
scenario.explanation: Light arrives almost instantly. Sound travels about 343 m each second, so 3 s × 343 m/s ≈ 1,030 m, roughly 1 km.

days.title: Pitch, Loudness and Hearing
days.content:
🎼 Frequency and Pitch

Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency → higher pitch. A tighter or shorter guitar string vibrates faster and sounds higher.

🔈 Amplitude and Loudness

Amplitude is how far the particles move from rest. Larger amplitude → louder sound. Loudness is measured in decibels (dB). Long exposure above about 85 dB (a busy road, loud videoke) can permanently damage hearing.

👂 What We Can Hear

  • Humans hear about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
  • Infrasound (below 20 Hz) — made by earthquakes and elephants.
  • Ultrasound (above 20,000 Hz) — used by bats, dolphins and medical scanners.

🏔️ Echoes

An echo is reflected sound. Hard, flat surfaces reflect sound strongly; soft, rough surfaces absorb it. Measuring the time an echo takes lets us calculate distance: distance = speed × time ÷ 2 (the sound goes there and back).

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each property or term to its meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.why: It decides the pitch of the sound.
A faster vibration sounds higher, like a whistle compared with a drum.
A bigger vibration carries more energy and sounds louder.
Sounds above about 85 dB for long periods can damage hearing.
Too high for humans to hear; used by bats and medical scanners.
Too low for humans to hear; produced by earthquakes and elephants.

match.right: Sound reflected from a hard surface
match.why: The reflected wave returns to the listener after a short delay.

match.right: Particles vibrate along the wave's direction
match.why: Sound moves as compressions and rarefactions through air.

days.title: Sound in Navigation and Medicine
days.content:
🚢 Sonar

SONAR (SOund Navigation And Ranging) sends a pulse of sound into water and times the echo. Fishing boats find schools of fish; ships measure the depth of the sea floor.

Example: an echo returns after 2.0 s in sea water (1,500 m/s). The sound traveled 1,500 × 2.0 = 3,000 m there and back, so the depth is 1,500 m.

🦇 Echolocation

Bats and dolphins send out ultrasound clicks and listen to the echoes to find food and avoid obstacles in the dark or in murky water.

🩺 Ultrasound in Medicine

An ultrasound probe sends high-frequency sound into the body. Echoes from organs and from a baby in the womb build a moving image. Unlike X-rays, ultrasound does not ionize cells, so it is safe for pregnant mothers. Strong focused ultrasound can also break kidney stones without surgery.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Apply echoes and frequency to real situations. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: A fishing boat's sonar pulse returns 0.4 s after it is sent. Sound travels 1,500 m/s in sea water. How deep is the school of fish?
scenario.explanation: The pulse travels down and back: 1,500 × 0.4 = 600 m in total, so the fish are 600 ÷ 2 = 300 m deep. 600 m forgets to divide by 2.

scenario.text: Why is ultrasound, not X-ray, used to check a baby in the womb?

choices.label: It forms images without ionizing cells
It travels faster than X-rays in the body
It shows bones more clearly than X-rays
It needs no gel or contact with the skin

scenario.explanation: Ultrasound is a mechanical wave that does not damage cells, so it is safe for a developing baby. X-rays are ionizing radiation.

scenario.text: A guitarist plucks the SAME string harder. What changes in the sound?

choices.label: Loudness increases; pitch stays the same
Pitch rises; loudness stays the same
The speed of the sound in air increases

scenario.explanation: Plucking harder gives a larger amplitude (louder). The string's length and tightness are unchanged, so its frequency (pitch) stays the same.

scenario.text: A bat flies through a dark cave without hitting the walls. Which explanation is correct?

choices.label: It times echoes of its own ultrasound calls
It sees the walls using infrared light
It feels air pressure from the walls
It hears the walls vibrating by themselves

scenario.explanation: Bats send ultrasound calls and listen to the echoes. The delay tells them how far away walls and insects are — this is echolocation.

scenario.text: A classroom echoes so much that students cannot hear the teacher clearly. Which change would help MOST?

choices.label: Add soft panels and curtains to the walls
Paint the walls with glossy enamel paint
Replace the wooden doors with steel doors
Open the windows only during the class

scenario.explanation: Soft, rough materials absorb sound instead of reflecting it, reducing echoes. Glossy paint and steel reflect sound even more.

days.title: Controlling Sound
days.content:
🔇 Soundproofing

Noise can be reduced in three ways:

  1. Absorb it — foam, acoustic tiles, carpets and curtains turn sound energy into a little heat.
  2. Block it — heavy, dense walls and double-glazed windows stop sound from passing through.
  3. Seal gaps — sound leaks through cracks under doors and around windows.

📢 Amplifiers

A microphone changes sound into an electrical signal. An amplifier increases the signal's amplitude, and a speaker changes it back into a louder sound. The pitch does not change — only the loudness.

🎧 Noise-Cancelling Headphones

A small microphone picks up outside noise and the headphones play an opposite wave (crest where the noise has a trough). The two waves cancel each other — this is destructive interference. It works best for steady sounds like a jeepney engine.

🧠 Reasoning Tip

Ask: is the problem the sound being made, reflected or passing through? Choose absorb, block or seal accordingly.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

escape.text: Which property of sound mainly decides its LOUDNESS?
escape.explanation: A larger amplitude means the particles vibrate more strongly, so the sound is louder. Frequency decides pitch.

escape.text: What range of frequencies can most humans hear?
escape.explanation: Normal human hearing covers roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sounds above it are ultrasound; below it, infrasound.

escape.text: What does an amplifier do to a sound signal?

choices.label: It slows down the sound wave

escape.explanation: An amplifier makes the signal bigger, so the speaker produces a louder sound with the same pitch.

escape.text: Noise-cancelling headphones play a wave that is the exact opposite of the outside noise. What happens?

choices.label: The waves cancel by destructive interference
The waves combine into a louder noise
The noise is reflected back to its source
The noise turns into an ultrasound wave

escape.explanation: When a crest meets a trough of equal size, they cancel. This destructive interference reduces the noise you hear.

escape.text: A family lives beside a busy highway. Which change will block the MOST traffic noise inside the house?

choices.label: Paint the outer walls a lighter color
Put a small fan beside the main door
Hang wind chimes near every window

escape.explanation: Dense, sealed double-glazed windows block sound from passing through. Paint color, fans and chimes do nothing to block noise.

escape.text: A videoke at a neighbor's party measures 100 dB for many hours. What is the main health risk?
escape.explanation: Long exposure above about 85 dB damages the tiny hair cells in the inner ear, which do not grow back.
